subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee Crosses the Red Sea
description: A micro-lesson that makes Coffee Crosses the Red Sea usable.

hook.text: Coffee left Africa sometime before the 15th century, crossing the Red Sea to Yemen.

buildup.text: Sufi monks in Yemen adopted coffee to fuel overnight devotional chanting. They called it qahwa.

discovery.text: Yemen became the world's first coffee cultivator, growing beans on terraced mountain farms.

twist.text: Yemenis guarded their monopoly fiercely. Exporting fertile beans was forbidden for over a century.

climax.text: The port of Mocha became synonymous with coffee. Ships carried beans to Persia, Egypt, and beyond.

punchline.text: From monks' prayers to global trade—Yemen launched it.

quiz.question: What was the port that became synonymous with coffee trade?

details.summary: Coffee traveled from Ethiopia across the Red Sea to Yemen, where it was first systematically cultivated. Yemeni traders and Sufi mystics transformed it from a wild plant into a cultivated crop and a traded commodity. Yemen became the world's first and for a time only commercial coffee producer.
details.whyItMatters: The crossing of the Red Sea was the moment coffee went from wild plant to commercial crop. Yemen's monopoly would shape trade routes and colonial ambitions for centuries.
takeaways: Coffee crossed from Ethiopia to Yemen across the Red Sea
Yemen was the first country to cultivate coffee commercially
Yemeni traders monopolized the coffee trade for over a century

faq.question: When did coffee arrive in Yemen from Ethiopia?
faq.answer: The timeline is uncertain, but most historians place it between the 1300s and 1400s. Trade across the Red Sea between Ethiopia and the Arabian Peninsula had existed for millennia, and coffee berries or plants likely traveled with traders or Sufi pilgrims.

faq.question: How did Yemen maintain its coffee monopoly?
faq.answer: Yemenis carefully controlled the export of viable coffee seeds, reportedly boiling or partially roasting all beans before sale to prevent germination. The port of Mocha became the sole outlet for Yemeni coffee to the world. The monopoly held until the Dutch smuggled plants out in the 1600s.
